ao_demand_evidence.input: Calculate the actual length of a 21 mm specimen image shown at ×300 magnification. Give the answer in μm.
Cell A has an image 12 mm long at ×200 and cell B has an image 15 mm long at ×500. Calculate the actual length of each cell and say which cell is larger.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: A is 12 ÷ 200 = 0.06 mm = 60 μm and B is 15 ÷ 500 = 0.03 mm = 30 μm. A is the larger cell, even though its image is shorter.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Suggest why an unfamiliar root cell with a visible cellulose wall but no chloroplasts can still be classified as a plant cell.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The wall is plant-cell evidence; roots are not normally exposed to light and need not contain chloroplasts, so absence of chloroplasts does not outweigh the wall.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Fig. VIS-6116-3.2-03 is a photomicrograph of plant cells from a temporary slide. Draw the cells you can see as a labelled line drawing.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: A correct drawing uses single, clear, unbroken outlines with no shading and shows the cells in their observed shapes and proportions. At least two visible structures, such as the cell wall, cytoplasm or nucleus, are correctly labelled. Each label line is drawn with a ruler and touches the structure named.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Fig. VIS-6116-3.2-04 is a photomicrograph of an animal tissue. Draw the cells as a labelled line drawing, showing how they are arranged and the nuclei that you can see.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: A correct drawing uses single, clear, unbroken outlines with no shading. It shows the cells packed in the arrangement seen in the photomicrograph, with a nucleus drawn in each cell where one is visible. Visible structures such as a nucleus or the cell membrane are labelled with ruled lines.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two cells of equal size receive the same oxygen supply. X must actively transport a much larger ion load per minute than Y. Suggest which is likely to contain more mitochondria and explain the link.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: X is likely to contain more mitochondria because its greater active-transport workload needs a higher rate of energy release through respiration.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Exchange unit X has twice the total surface area of Y, but an impermeable coat covers three-quarters of X. Y is fully exposed and other conditions match. Describe how the total diffusion rates compare.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: X has only half Y’s effective exposed area, because twice the area with a quarter exposed is half, so its total diffusion rate is expected to be lower.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A solute spreads faster in a cool shaken container than in a warm still container. A learner says this shows temperature does not affect diffusion. Describe why this conclusion is not justified.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The comparison does not isolate temperature because shaking adds bulk mixing. Faster spread in the cool container therefore does not disprove the effect of temperature on diffusion.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two matched membrane systems are compared. In A the concentrations are 8 and 2 units on opposite sides; in B they are 8 and 6 units. Describe which should have faster net diffusion.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: A has the steeper difference, 6 units compared with 2 units for B, so faster net diffusion is expected if permeability and other conditions match.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Fluid collects between an oxygen source and some cells, so the total diffusion path increases from 4 μm to 12 μm. Other factors match. Describe the likely change in the rate of oxygen diffusion.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Exchange is expected to slow because the total path is now three times longer.

ao_demand_evidence.input: In the litmus demonstration the times to turn blue are 10 s, 25 s and 46 s at increasing distances. Suggest why these times do not by themselves show that particles move at a constant speed along the tube.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The litmus response is an arrival endpoint and diffusion is random motion, not a directed stream at one speed. The time differences, 15 s then 21 s, are not equal, so they do not support a constant-speed model.

ao_demand_evidence.input: In an investigation the time for a dye to reach a fixed point falls as temperature rises, and the volume of water and the colour endpoint are the same in every trial. Suggest what this shows.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The shorter times show faster diffusion to the same endpoint, consistent with greater particle kinetic energy at higher temperature, provided other relevant conditions were controlled.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two enzyme chains contain the same number of amino acids, but the amino acids are in a different order. Explain why they could act on different substrates.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Different order can cause different folding and active-site shapes. The substrates that fit those sites can therefore differ despite equal chain length.

ao_demand_evidence.input: An extract made with four times as much tissue gives a stronger sugar-test response. Suggest why this does not show that its region has more sugar per gram.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The stronger response may result from the greater tissue mass rather than a higher sugar content per gram. Standardise mass and extraction volume before comparing.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Enzyme X acts on substrate P but not on substrate Q, which is a similar size but has a different shape where it would bind. Explain why.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: P can interact correctly with X’s active site, whereas Q’s binding region does not fit/interact suitably. Similar overall size alone does not establish substrate compatibility.

ao_demand_evidence.input: One sample of an enzyme was chilled and another was heated enough to denature it. Both are then returned to 25 °C. Explain the likely difference between the two samples.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The chilled sample can regain activity as particles move faster again. The denatured sample is expected to remain less active because its active-site shape was altered, not simply slowed.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two enzymes are tested at pH 2. One has an optimum near pH 2 and the other has an optimum near pH 7. Explain why they need not have equal activity.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The first is near its suitable optimum; the second is far from its optimum and may have impaired binding or denaturation. Different enzymes have different pH requirements.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Suggest why a lipase trial starting at a lower pH can reach an indicator’s colour endpoint sooner even if it does not produce fatty acid faster.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: It may need a smaller further pH change to reach that endpoint. Endpoint times from different starting pH values therefore do not necessarily measure comparable acid-production rates.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A biological powder removes a protein stain. Suggest why this does not show that the same enzyme removes an oily stain equally well.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The enzyme may be a protease with specificity for protein substrates. Oil is a different material and may need a lipase or other cleaning action.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why photosynthesis may fall in a green leaf whose air spaces have become water-filled. Its chlorophyll content and illumination are unchanged; gases diffuse more slowly through water than air.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Water in the spaces slows carbon dioxide diffusion to mesophyll cells; reduced carbon dioxide supply can limit photosynthesis.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain what these seedling results show about the cause of the pale leaves. All solutions lack iron; half receive iron at week 2 and turn green, while matched untreated plants remain pale. Other conditions are the same.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The recovery supports iron deficiency as the cause of paleness; iron addition permits chlorophyll formation, unlike the untreated comparison.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why a shaded seedling and a magnesium-deficient seedling may both grow slowly, although moving them into bright light helps just the shaded one. Water and other nutrients are sufficient.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The shaded plant lacked light; the deficient plant lacks magnesium for chlorophyll, so extra light does not replace the missing chlorophyll constituent.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Seedlings grown in a complete solution have a mean root length of 8.2 cm. Matched seedlings in a solution lacking only phosphate have a mean root length of 3.4 cm. Each treatment has ten seedlings, with the same light and temperature. Explain what conclusion these results support.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The mean root length is 4.8 cm shorter without phosphate, so the results support the conclusion that phosphate shortage reduced root growth; phosphate is needed for the DNA and ATP used to make new cells.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why supplying extra light did not restore growth in seedlings whose solution contained no nitrate, although their leaves still made carbohydrate.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Extra light cannot supply nitrogen; without nitrate the seedlings cannot make sufficient amino acids and proteins for growth.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Fig. VIS-6116-3.6.1.3-10 is a graph of photosynthesis rate against light intensity at a fixed temperature. One curve rises and then levels off at high light intensity. A second curve, obtained at the same temperature but a higher carbon dioxide concentration, rises above the plateau of the first curve at high light intensity. Explain which factor limited the rate at the plateau of the first curve.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The first curve is flat at high light intensity, so more light gave no rise in rate and light was not the limit there. Raising carbon dioxide alone allowed a higher rate at the same light intensity, so carbon dioxide concentration was the limiting factor at the plateau.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why a growing teenager may need more protein relative to body mass than a non-growing adult of similar activity, even though the adult is heavier.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The teenager needs amino acids for new tissue as well as repair; the adult mainly maintains existing tissue, so body mass alone does not settle the relative requirement.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why equal energy needs do not imply equal iron needs for two adults of the same mass and activity when one has regular menstrual blood loss and the other does not.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Energy and iron are separate needs, so similar energy needs say nothing about iron; the person losing blood must replace the iron lost in haemoglobin and so needs more iron.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why a worker who changes from carrying sacks all day to seated duties may gain fat if food intake remains unchanged for months. Assume other conditions remain similar.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The new duties reduce energy expenditure; continued intake above expenditure supplies surplus energy stored as fat.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why simply adding more cooking oil would not correct both extra energy needs and low iron intake during pregnancy.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Oil supplies energy but little iron; the extra haemoglobin requirement still needs an appropriate iron source.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why extra sweetened drinks alone would not make a low-protein diet adequate for a breastfeeding mother, even if the drinks supplied the extra energy.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Sugar can supply energy but not amino acids; protein is still needed to make milk proteins and maintain maternal tissues.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Suggest why famine risk may rise in an isolated district after flooding even when the country’s total grain supply is adequate. The district’s main road and stored harvest have been destroyed.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The flood removed local food reserves; damaged transport prevents national supplies reaching the district, so total availability does not guarantee local access.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why a person with cholera may continue losing large volumes of watery stool after eating very little. The toxin causes chloride ions to enter the small intestine.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Water follows the secreted ions from body fluids into the intestine by osmosis; the fluid loss therefore need not come from food just eaten.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Suggest why a muscle must consume glucose faster if its energy supply shifts from aerobic to anaerobic respiration but its energy demand stays unchanged.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Anaerobic respiration releases much less energy from each glucose molecule. More glucose must therefore be broken down each minute to supply the same energy.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain the likely bend of a young shoot when a treatment makes its left side elongate 4 mm and its right side elongate 1 mm during the same period.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: It bends towards the right. The left side grows 3 mm more, so it becomes the longer outside of the curve.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why the second neurone stops responding when impulses still reach the end of the first neurone but a chemical stops neurotransmitter being released. The receptors are not affected.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The impulse is electrical and cannot cross the gap without neurotransmitter. With no transmitter binding, the receptors on the second neurone are not stimulated, so it does not respond.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why a pupil cannot narrow in bright light if the circular muscles of the iris cannot contract, although the radial muscles relax normally.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The pupil narrows only when the circular muscles contract. Relaxing the radial muscles alone does not pull the pupil smaller, so it stays wide.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why an older person whose lens has become stiff cannot focus on a near object, even though the ciliary muscles contract and the suspensory ligaments slacken.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: A stiff lens cannot become thicker and more curved, so it cannot refract light more. The near object is therefore not focused on the retina.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why an eye cannot focus on a distant object if its suspensory ligaments are damaged and cannot pull on the lens, even though the ciliary muscles relax.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The lens is not pulled thinner and flatter. It stays thick, so it refracts light too strongly and the distant object is not focused on the retina.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Suggest which control system best fits each observation: response X begins almost immediately after a skin stimulus and ends quickly; response Y follows a blood-borne signal and persists for hours.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: X fits nervous control because it is rapid and brief. Y fits hormonal control because the signal travels in blood and its effect lasts a long time.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain which culture is directly affected by medicine K: K blocks bacterial cell-wall formation; culture A contains susceptible bacteria and culture B contains viruses inside animal cells.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: K affects culture A, because its bacteria make cell walls and K blocks this. The viruses in culture B have no bacterial cell wall, so K does not affect them.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why route X presents a greater blood-borne infection risk than route Y: X reuses a syringe containing another person’s blood; Y uses new sterile equipment with no shared preparation equipment.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: X can inject another person’s infected blood directly into the next user. Y uses new sterile equipment, so there is no blood from another person to carry the virus.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Suggest why, when adrenaline is released in a person whose liver glycogen store has been used up, the pulse rate rises but blood glucose does not.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Adrenaline acts on the heart, so the pulse rate still rises. Adrenaline raises blood glucose by causing the liver to break down glycogen; with the store used up there is no glycogen to convert, so blood glucose does not rise.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why a heating controller that switches on extra heating whenever a room becomes too warm, and still more heating as the temperature rises, is not an example of negative feedback.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Its response adds to the temperature rise instead of opposing it. The temperature therefore moves further from the set level and is not brought back to normal.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Calculate the actual length of a 21 mm specimen image shown at ×300 magnification. Give the answer in μm.
Cell A has an image 12 mm long at ×200 and cell B has an image 15 mm long at ×500. Calculate the actual length of each cell and say which cell is larger.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: A is 12 ÷ 200 = 0.06 mm = 60 μm and B is 15 ÷ 500 = 0.03 mm = 30 μm. A is the larger cell, even though its image is shorter.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Suggest why an unfamiliar root cell with a visible cellulose wall but no chloroplasts can still be classified as a plant cell.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The wall is plant-cell evidence; roots are not normally exposed to light and need not contain chloroplasts, so absence of chloroplasts does not outweigh the wall.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Fig. VIS-6116-3.2-03 is a photomicrograph of plant cells from a temporary slide. Draw the cells you can see as a labelled line drawing.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: A correct drawing uses single, clear, unbroken outlines with no shading and shows the cells in their observed shapes and proportions. At least two visible structures, such as the cell wall, cytoplasm or nucleus, are correctly labelled. Each label line is drawn with a ruler and touches the structure named.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Fig. VIS-6116-3.2-04 is a photomicrograph of an animal tissue. Draw the cells as a labelled line drawing, showing how they are arranged and the nuclei that you can see.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: A correct drawing uses single, clear, unbroken outlines with no shading. It shows the cells packed in the arrangement seen in the photomicrograph, with a nucleus drawn in each cell where one is visible. Visible structures such as a nucleus or the cell membrane are labelled with ruled lines.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two cells of equal size receive the same oxygen supply. X must actively transport a much larger ion load per minute than Y. Suggest which is likely to contain more mitochondria and explain the link.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: X is likely to contain more mitochondria because its greater active-transport workload needs a higher rate of energy release through respiration.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Exchange unit X has twice the total surface area of Y, but an impermeable coat covers three-quarters of X. Y is fully exposed and other conditions match. Describe how the total diffusion rates compare.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: X has only half Y’s effective exposed area, because twice the area with a quarter exposed is half, so its total diffusion rate is expected to be lower.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A solute spreads faster in a cool shaken container than in a warm still container. A learner says this shows temperature does not affect diffusion. Describe why this conclusion is not justified.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The comparison does not isolate temperature because shaking adds bulk mixing. Faster spread in the cool container therefore does not disprove the effect of temperature on diffusion.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two matched membrane systems are compared. In A the concentrations are 8 and 2 units on opposite sides; in B they are 8 and 6 units. Describe which should have faster net diffusion.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: A has the steeper difference, 6 units compared with 2 units for B, so faster net diffusion is expected if permeability and other conditions match.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Fluid collects between an oxygen source and some cells, so the total diffusion path increases from 4 μm to 12 μm. Other factors match. Describe the likely change in the rate of oxygen diffusion.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Exchange is expected to slow because the total path is now three times longer.

ao_demand_evidence.input: In the litmus demonstration the times to turn blue are 10 s, 25 s and 46 s at increasing distances. Suggest why these times do not by themselves show that particles move at a constant speed along the tube.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The litmus response is an arrival endpoint and diffusion is random motion, not a directed stream at one speed. The time differences, 15 s then 21 s, are not equal, so they do not support a constant-speed model.

ao_demand_evidence.input: In an investigation the time for a dye to reach a fixed point falls as temperature rises, and the volume of water and the colour endpoint are the same in every trial. Suggest what this shows.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The shorter times show faster diffusion to the same endpoint, consistent with greater particle kinetic energy at higher temperature, provided other relevant conditions were controlled.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two enzyme chains contain the same number of amino acids, but the amino acids are in a different order. Explain why they could act on different substrates.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: Different order can cause different folding and active-site shapes. The substrates that fit those sites can therefore differ despite equal chain length.

ao_demand_evidence.input: An extract made with four times as much tissue gives a stronger sugar-test response. Suggest why this does not show that its region has more sugar per gram.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The stronger response may result from the greater tissue mass rather than a higher sugar content per gram. Standardise mass and extraction volume before comparing.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Enzyme X acts on substrate P but not on substrate Q, which is a similar size but has a different shape where it would bind. Explain why.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: P can interact correctly with X’s active site, whereas Q’s binding region does not fit/interact suitably. Similar overall size alone does not establish substrate compatibility.

ao_demand_evidence.input: One sample of an enzyme was chilled and another was heated enough to denature it. Both are then returned to 25 °C. Explain the likely difference between the two samples.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The chilled sample can regain activity as particles move faster again. The denatured sample is expected to remain less active because its active-site shape was altered, not simply slowed.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Two enzymes are tested at pH 2. One has an optimum near pH 2 and the other has an optimum near pH 7. Explain why they need not have equal activity.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The first is near its suitable optimum; the second is far from its optimum and may have impaired binding or denaturation. Different enzymes have different pH requirements.

ao_demand_evidence.input: Suggest why a lipase trial starting at a lower pH can reach an indicator’s colour endpoint sooner even if it does not produce fatty acid faster.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: It may need a smaller further pH change to reach that endpoint. Endpoint times from different starting pH values therefore do not necessarily measure comparable acid-production rates.

ao_demand_evidence.input: A biological powder removes a protein stain. Suggest why this does not show that the same enzyme removes an oily stain equally well.
ao_demand_evidence.inference_or_processing: The enzyme may be a protease with specificity for protein substrates. Oil is a different material and may need a lipase or other cleaning action.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why photosynthesis may fall in a green leaf whose air spaces have become water-filled. Its chlorophyll content and illumination are unchanged; gases diffuse more slowly through water than air.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Water in the spaces slows carbon dioxide diffusion to mesophyll cells; reduced carbon dioxide supply can limit photosynthesis.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain what these seedling results show about the cause of the pale leaves. All solutions lack iron; half receive iron at week 2 and turn green, while matched untreated plants remain pale. Other conditions are the same.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The recovery supports iron deficiency as the cause of paleness; iron addition permits chlorophyll formation, unlike the untreated comparison.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why a shaded seedling and a magnesium-deficient seedling may both grow slowly, although moving them into bright light helps just the shaded one. Water and other nutrients are sufficient.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The shaded plant lacked light; the deficient plant lacks magnesium for chlorophyll, so extra light does not replace the missing chlorophyll constituent.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Seedlings grown in a complete solution have a mean root length of 8.2 cm. Matched seedlings in a solution lacking only phosphate have a mean root length of 3.4 cm. Each treatment has ten seedlings, with the same light and temperature. Explain what conclusion these results support.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The mean root length is 4.8 cm shorter without phosphate, so the results support the conclusion that phosphate shortage reduced root growth; phosphate is needed for the DNA and ATP used to make new cells.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why supplying extra light did not restore growth in seedlings whose solution contained no nitrate, although their leaves still made carbohydrate.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Extra light cannot supply nitrogen; without nitrate the seedlings cannot make sufficient amino acids and proteins for growth.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Fig. VIS-6116-3.6.1.3-10 is a graph of photosynthesis rate against light intensity at a fixed temperature. One curve rises and then levels off at high light intensity. A second curve, obtained at the same temperature but a higher carbon dioxide concentration, rises above the plateau of the first curve at high light intensity. Explain which factor limited the rate at the plateau of the first curve.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The first curve is flat at high light intensity, so more light gave no rise in rate and light was not the limit there. Raising carbon dioxide alone allowed a higher rate at the same light intensity, so carbon dioxide concentration was the limiting factor at the plateau.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why a growing teenager may need more protein relative to body mass than a non-growing adult of similar activity, even though the adult is heavier.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The teenager needs amino acids for new tissue as well as repair; the adult mainly maintains existing tissue, so body mass alone does not settle the relative requirement.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why equal energy needs do not imply equal iron needs for two adults of the same mass and activity when one has regular menstrual blood loss and the other does not.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Energy and iron are separate needs, so similar energy needs say nothing about iron; the person losing blood must replace the iron lost in haemoglobin and so needs more iron.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why a worker who changes from carrying sacks all day to seated duties may gain fat if food intake remains unchanged for months. Assume other conditions remain similar.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The new duties reduce energy expenditure; continued intake above expenditure supplies surplus energy stored as fat.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why simply adding more cooking oil would not correct both extra energy needs and low iron intake during pregnancy.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Oil supplies energy but little iron; the extra haemoglobin requirement still needs an appropriate iron source.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why extra sweetened drinks alone would not make a low-protein diet adequate for a breastfeeding mother, even if the drinks supplied the extra energy.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Sugar can supply energy but not amino acids; protein is still needed to make milk proteins and maintain maternal tissues.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Suggest why famine risk may rise in an isolated district after flooding even when the country’s total grain supply is adequate. The district’s main road and stored harvest have been destroyed.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The flood removed local food reserves; damaged transport prevents national supplies reaching the district, so total availability does not guarantee local access.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why a person with cholera may continue losing large volumes of watery stool after eating very little. The toxin causes chloride ions to enter the small intestine.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: Water follows the secreted ions from body fluids into the intestine by osmosis; the fluid loss therefore need not come from food just eaten.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: B: consequential reasoning from the given constraints/results; not the scenario name alone.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why a pupil cannot narrow in bright light if the circular muscles of the iris cannot contract, although the radial muscles relax normally.
ao_demand_evidence.inference: The pupil narrows only when the circular muscles contract. Relaxing the radial muscles alone does not pull the pupil smaller, so it stays wide.
ao_demand_evidence.classification: reasoning from the supplied case, rather than a renamed recall prompt.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why an older person whose lens has become stiff cannot focus on a near object, even though the ciliary muscles contract and the suspensory ligaments slacken.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Explain why route X presents a greater blood-borne infection risk than route Y: X reuses a syringe containing another person’s blood; Y uses new sterile equipment with no shared preparation equipment.

ao_demand_evidence.new_input: Suggest why, when adrenaline is released in a person whose liver glycogen store has been used up, the pulse rate rises but blood glucose does not.
